derived_from.quoted_text: No acknowledgment or promise is sufficient evidence of a new or continuing contract, by which to take the case out of the operation of this title, unless the same is contained in some writing, signed by the party to be charged thereby; but any payment of any principal or interest due on any promissory note ... shall be deemed a sufficient acknowledgment or promise of a continuing contract to stop, from time to time as any such payment is made, the running of the time within which an action may be commenced upon such note ... provided, however, that no payment of itself shall revive a cause of action once barred.
derived_from.tier_rationale: Added 2026-08-30 (round 21) to encode the revival-timing rule the corroboration pipeline's adversarial check found missing: a payment made BEFORE the limitations period runs restarts the clock, but a payment made AFTER the debt is already time-barred does NOT revive it -- only a signed written acknowledgment or new promise can. Where a complaint was already filed, the relevant comparison is accrual-plus-4-years against the FILING date, not today; where a judgment already exists, the relevant period is this 10-year enforcement/renewal period, not the original 4-year contract SOL at all. logic.applies_to: actions on a contract/obligation founded on a written instrument -- most credit-card cardmember agreements and signed loan/retail-installment contracts
logic.accrual: Generally the date of default/breach or last payment, a fact question this node does not itself resolve. CAUTION: for a deficiency claim after repossession/foreclosure sale of secured collateral, accrual is frequently measured from the disposition/deficiency date, not the last payment date -- applying a flat 'last payment' accrual rule to a secured installment contract can understate the time remaining and produce a false 'time-barred' conclusion. Flagged as a fact-sensitive distinction this node does not fully resolve; a dedicated secured-transactions SOL node is HORIZON work.
logic.affirmative_bar_note: subdivision (d) is notable and California-specific: once the period has run, a creditor is statutorily barred from even INITIATING suit or arbitration to collect -- this is stronger than a mere affirmative defense the debtor must raise, though the debtor should still plead it.
logic.determination: expired_if [complaint-filing date, or today if no complaint has yet been filed] > (accrual_date + 4 years), subject to any tolling not yet encoded (tolling nodes not yet built for CA). CRITICAL: this determination is NOT the right question at all once a lawsuit has already been filed or a judgment already exists -- see filing_date_vs_today_note and judgment_enforcement_note.
logic.choice_of_law_note: If the underlying contract designates the law of another state and the cause of action arose there (e.g., a credit-card agreement issued from the creditor's home state), CCP § 361 (California's borrowing statute) can require applying that state's shorter limitations period instead of this 4-year period. This node does not itself resolve the choice-of-law or where-the-claim-arose analysis -- flagged as a threshold fact question.
logic.revival_note: A payment made BEFORE the 4-year period expires restarts the clock (CCP § 360). A payment made AFTER the period has already expired does NOT revive the claim -- only a signed written acknowledgment or new promise does. Whether a given payment came before or after the bar is itself a fact question this node does not resolve without the specific dates.

drafting_revisions.summary: Fixed 'determination' to key off the complaint's filing date (not today) once a suit has been filed, and flagged that an existing judgment is governed by CCP 683.020's 10-year enforcement/renewal period rather than the original 4-year SOL at all; added filing_date_vs_today_note, judgment_enforcement_note, and installment_separate_accrual_note; added 2 checklist items.

logic.filing_date_vs_today_note: If a complaint has already been filed (or a default judgment already entered), the relevant comparison for whether the SUIT was timely is accrual-plus-4-years against the date the COMPLAINT WAS FILED, not against today's date. A consumer sued in 2022 on a 2019 default, who asks in 2026 whether the case is time-barred, should NOT be told the suit is expired merely because today is more than 4 years past accrual -- the suit was timely when filed in 2022, and the SOL question is now moot as to that filing (whatever other defenses may exist). Applying today's-date logic to an already-filed or already-judgment case produces a materially wrong answer.
logic.judgment_enforcement_note: Once a judgment has actually been entered (including a default judgment), the ORIGINAL 4-year contract statute of limitations no longer governs anything -- the judgment itself is enforceable for 10 years from entry, renewable for additional 10-year periods without limit, under CCP § 683.020. A consumer with an old judgment against them should not be told the judgment is 'expired' or unenforceable based on the 4-year contract SOL; the judgment-enforcement clock is separate and starts over at entry (and again at each renewal).
logic.installment_separate_accrual_note: This node's single-accrual-date framing assumes the debt is due in full as of one date. For an INSTALLMENT obligation (e.g., a written personal loan or payment plan with scheduled periodic payments) where the creditor has NOT invoked an acceleration clause, California law runs the 4-year period separately on EACH missed installment as it comes due -- not from a single default or last-payment date. A creditor suing in 2026 on an installment loan where payments stopped in 2019 may still timely sue for installments that came due within the last 4 years, even though installments from 2019-2021 are barred. This node's single-accrual-date determination, applied to an unaccelerated installment obligation, would incorrectly declare the entire claim either wholly barred or wholly live rather than partially barred.

completeness_checklist.fact: Date of last payment on the debt, or date of default/breach if no payments were made
Whether the underlying contract is written (this node, 4 years) or oral/unwritten (see CA-SOL-ORAL-CONTRACT-DEBT, 2 years) -- classification itself can be fact-intensive for revolving credit accounts
Any facts suggesting tolling (e.g., debtor's absence from the state under CCP § 351, other statutory tolling) -- flagged, not resolved by this node
Whether the underlying contract designates another state's law, and whether the claim arose in that state (CCP § 361 borrowing statute may apply a shorter foreign limitations period)
Whether this is a deficiency claim following repossession or foreclosure sale of secured collateral (accrual may run from the disposition/deficiency date, not last payment)

If any payment was made after the last default, whether it was made before or after the 4-year period had already run (only a payment made before the bar restarts the clock; one made after does not revive it without a signed written acknowledgment)

Whether a complaint has already been filed (compare filing date, not today, to accrual + 4 years) or a judgment already entered (the governing period becomes the 10-year CCP § 683.020 enforcement/renewal period, not the original 4-year contract SOL)
Whether the obligation is an installment contract that was never accelerated -- if so, the 4-year period runs separately on each missed installment, not from a single accrual/last-payment date

consequences_and_next_steps.action: If the 4-year period has run and no tolling applies, raise statute of limitations as an affirmative defense in the Answer; also note CCP § 337(d)'s bar on the creditor even initiating collection litigation.
If close to the 4-year line, confirm the exact accrual date, the written/oral classification, and check for tolling facts before relying on this defense.

nodes.title: California statute of limitations on an oral/unwritten-contract consumer-debt lawsuit

derived_from.quoted_text: Within two years: 1. derived_from.quoted_text: An action is commenced, within the meaning of this Title, when the complaint is filed.
derived_from.tier_rationale: Added 2026-08-30 (round 21) to fix the accrual-comparison logic bug the corroboration pipeline's adversarial check found: 'expired' should be measured against the complaint's FILING date, not 'today's date' -- a suit that was timely filed can be wrongly reported as time-barred if the comparison instead uses the date the consumer is asking the question (which is often after filing, at or after service). logic.applies_to: actions on a contract/obligation NOT founded on a written instrument
logic.accrual: generally the date of default/breach or last payment, a fact question this node does not itself resolve
logic.note: much shorter than the 4-year written-contract period (CA-SOL-WRITTEN-CONTRACT-DEBT) -- whether a specific debt (e.g., an open-book retail account, a verbal loan between individuals) counts as written or oral is itself a threshold fact question with real consequences and is not resolved by this node.
logic.determination: expired_if (complaint filing date, per CCP § 350 -- NOT today's date) > (accrual_date + 2 years), subject to any tolling not yet encoded beyond the § 351 caveat above
logic.classification_note: Credit card and other revolving retail accounts are the single most common CA consumer-debt scenario, and the mere absence of a document the consumer can locate does NOT make the debt 'oral' for SOL purposes -- such accounts are usually governed by the 4-year period under CCP § 337 (written contract, or an open book account/account stated) rather than this node's 2-year period. A consumer who cannot find a signed agreement should NOT be assumed to be under this node without confirming there is genuinely no written cardmember agreement, account terms, or running book-account record -- see CA-SOL-WRITTEN-CONTRACT-DEBT. This node is for genuinely unwritten obligations (e.g., a purely verbal personal loan).
logic.tolling_note: CCP § 351 tolls the 2-year period while the debtor is absent from California, but courts have held it unconstitutional as applied to out-of-state defendants engaged in interstate commerce, and it does not apply to corporations, limited partnerships, or nonresident motorists (Abramson v. Brownstein, 897 F.2d 389 (9th Cir. 1990)). Do NOT apply a flat day-for-day tolling add-on without confirming the debtor's absence falls within § 351's actual, constitutionally-valid scope. Bankruptcy automatic-stay tolling (11 U.S.C. § 362/108) and emergency court-order tolling are separate mechanisms, also not yet encoded here.

completeness_checklist.fact: Date of last payment on the debt, or date of default/breach if no payments were made
Confirmation the underlying obligation is genuinely NOT founded on a written instrument (vs. CA-SOL-WRITTEN-CONTRACT-DEBT)

Whether there is genuinely no written cardmember agreement, account terms, or book-account record for this debt (vs. simply not being able to locate one) -- credit card/revolving accounts are usually 4-year written-contract debts, not 2-year oral debts

Whether the debtor was absent from California after the debt accrued, AND whether that absence falls within CCP § 351's actual scope (it does not apply to interstate-commerce defendants, corporations, LPs, or nonresident motorists)
The date the collection complaint was actually FILED (not today's date, and not the service date, which often lags filing)

consequences_and_next_steps.action: If the 2-year period has run and no tolling applies, raise statute of limitations as an affirmative defense in the Answer.

nodes.title: California cap on wage garnishment for a consumer-debt judgment

derived_from.quoted_text: Except as otherwise provided in this chapter, the maximum amount of disposable earnings of an individual judgment debtor for any workweek that is subject to levy under an earnings withholding order shall not exceed the lesser of the following: (1) Twenty percent of the individual's disposable earnings for that week. (2) Forty percent of the amount by which the individual's disposable earnings for that week exceed 48 times the state minimum hourly wage in effect at the time the earnings are payable. If a judgment debtor works in a location where the local minimum hourly wage is greater than the state minimum hourly wage, the local minimum hourly wage in effect at the time the earnings are payable shall be used for the calculation made pursuant to this paragraph.

logic.formula: min(20% of weekly disposable earnings, 40% of (weekly disposable earnings - 48 x applicable minimum hourly wage))
logic.applicable_minimum_wage: the greater of the state minimum hourly wage or a higher local minimum wage where the debtor works, in effect when earnings are payable
logic.effective_date: 2023-09-01 -- this is CA's post-SB 1477 formula, materially more debtor-protective than the pre-2023 25%-of-disposable-earnings federal-conforming formula and more protective than the federal CCPA floor
logic.note_needs_current_figure: this node encodes the FORMULA verbatim; it does NOT itself contain the current state or local minimum-hourly-wage figure needed to compute a dollar result -- that figure changes periodically (state minimum wage schedule, and per-locality ordinances) and must be pulled current at time of use, not hardcoded here.
logic.determination: max_weekly_garnishment = the lesser of the two prongs above; anything withheld beyond that is unlawful

completeness_checklist.fact: Debtor's weekly disposable earnings
Current state minimum hourly wage, and any higher local minimum wage applicable where the debtor works, in effect at the time earnings are payable
Pay period (this node states the weekly formula; CCP § 706.050(b) has multiplier conversions for daily/biweekly/semimonthly/monthly periods not yet separately encoded)

consequences_and_next_steps.action: If an earnings withholding order exceeds the lesser-of formula above, object/move to modify the withholding order citing CCP § 706.050.

nodes.title: California homestead exemption from creditor forced sale of a residence

derived_from.quoted_text: (a) The amount of the homestead exemption is the greater of the following: (1) The countywide median sale price for a single-family home in the calendar year prior to the calendar year in which the judgment debtor claims the exemption, not to exceed six hundred thousand dollars ($600,000). (b) The amounts specified in this section shall adjust annually for inflation, beginning on January 1, 2022, based on the change in the annual California Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers, published by the Department of Industrial Relations, for the most recent one-year period ending on December 31 preceding the adjustment, with each adjusted amount rounded to the nearest twenty-five dollars ($25).

logic.exemption_amount: greater of (countywide median single-family home sale price in the prior calendar year, capped at $600,000) or $300,000, both figures inflation-adjusted annually from a 2022 base

Debtor's county, to look up the current countywide median single-family home sale price for the prior calendar year
Current inflation-adjusted dollar figures for the $300,000 floor and $600,000 cap

consequences_and_next_steps.action: If a creditor is attempting to force the sale of the debtor's home, claim the homestead exemption up to the computed amount citing CCP § 704.730 (and the surrounding procedural sections governing how the exemption is claimed and a forced-sale surplus is handled, not yet encoded).

nodes.title: California motor-vehicle equity exemption from creditor levy

derived_from.quoted_text: (a) Any combination of the following is exempt in the amount of seven thousand five hundred dollars ($7,500): (1) The aggregate equity in motor vehicles. (d) If the judgment debtor has only one motor vehicle and it is sold at an execution sale, the proceeds of the execution sale are exempt in the amount of seven thousand five hundred dollars ($7,500) without making a claim. The levying officer shall consult and may rely upon the records of the Department of Motor Vehicles in determining whether the judgment debtor has only one motor vehicle. In the case covered by this subdivision, the exemption provided by subdivision (a) is not available.

logic.applies_to: aggregate equity across a debtor's motor vehicles, or execution-sale proceeds, or insurance/indemnification proceeds for a vehicle -- combined, not stacked separately
logic.automatic_single_vehicle_case: if the debtor has only one vehicle and it is sold at execution sale, the $7,500 exemption on the proceeds applies automatically without the debtor filing a claim
logic.determination: up to $7,500 of vehicle equity/proceeds is protected from levy; equity above that amount remains reachable
logic.tools_of_trade_note: If the vehicle is reasonably necessary to and actually used in the debtor's trade, business, or profession, CCP § 704.060 provides a separate tools-of-trade exemption (aggregate ~$8,725, with the motor vehicle portion capped lower, ~$4,850) that can apply INSTEAD of, or alongside, this node's general § 704.010 vehicle exemption for a separate personal vehicle -- but § 704.060 itself says a trade vehicle is not separately exempt under it if an adequate § 704.010 vehicle is already available. This node alone, applied to a work vehicle without checking § 704.060, can materially understate the debtor's protection.
logic.bankruptcy_alternative_note: This $7,500 figure is the non-bankruptcy (CCP § 704 series) exemption. A debtor filing Chapter 7 bankruptcy may instead elect California's 'System 2' exemptions under CCP § 703.140(b), which includes a separate ~$8,625 vehicle exemption PLUS a wildcard (up to ~$1,950, plus any entirely-unused portion of the ~$36,750 homestead exemption -- e.g. a renter with no homestead claim) that can be stacked onto vehicle equity. System 2 is an all-or-nothing election in place of § 704, not a add-on to it. This node does not itself determine which system is more favorable for a given debtor.
logic.proceeds_time_limit_note: The execution-sale/insurance-proceeds branch of this exemption (CCP § 704.010(b)) is exempt only for 90 days after the debtor actually receives the proceeds -- after that, the money loses this specific protection (though it may still be protected as exempt personal property or under another exemption depending on how it was used or where it is held).

derived_from.quoted_text: (a) For the purposes of this section: (1) 'Deposit account' means a deposit account in which payments of public benefits or social security benefits are directly deposited by the government or its agent ... (b) Subject to the conditions specified in this section, the minimum amount specified in one of the following, whichever is applicable, that is on deposit in an account described in subdivision (a) is exempt without making a claim: (1) One thousand seven hundred fifty dollars ($1,750) where the account is a deposit account described in paragraph (2) of subdivision (a) [public benefits], and there is only one depositor ... (2) Two thousand six hundred dollars ($2,600) ... two or more depositors ... (3) Three thousand five hundred dollars ($3,500) where the account is a deposit account described in paragraph (3) of subdivision (a) [social security benefits], and there is only one depositor ... (4) Five thousand two hundred fifty dollars ($5,250) ... two or more depositors.
derived_from.tier_rationale: Added 2026-08-30 (round 21) to encode the much larger, separate automatic exemption for accounts receiving directly-deposited public benefits or Social Security payments, which the corroboration pipeline's adversarial check found missing (the node previously only encoded the smaller general § 704.220 minimum-balance exemption, leaving public-benefits/SSA recipients -- a very common fact pattern -- materially understated). Figures paraphrased/condensed at the '...' for brevity; confirmed via WebSearch cross-referencing current leginfo/FindLaw/Justia mirrors this session. Direct web_fetch of leginfo.legislature.ca.gov timed out repeatedly this session -- flagged for live re-verification, same caveat as other leginfo entries this round. Federal law (31 C.F.R. Part 212, the Treasury 'Garnishment of Accounts Containing Federal Benefit Payments' rule) separately and automatically protects roughly two months' worth of certain federal benefit payments received by direct deposit within a look-back period, regardless of state law -- flagged as a related but not-yet-independently-encoded federal protection, not asserted as verified statutory text in this round.

derived_from.quoted_text: The exemptions provided by this chapter apply only to property of a natural person.
derived_from.tier_rationale: Added 2026-08-30 (round 21) to encode the natural-person-only threshold the corroboration pipeline's adversarial check found missing -- an LLC, corporation, or other entity judgment debtor gets NO protection under this node (or any CCP § 704 exemption) at all. Same sourcing basis/caveat as other leginfo entries this round.

derived_from.quoted_text: 'Paid earnings' means earnings, as defined in Section 706.011, that were paid to the employee during the 30-day period ending on the date of the levy ... (b) All of the paid earnings ... are exempt if, prior to payment to the employee, they were subject to an earnings withholding order or an earnings assignment order for support. (c) Seventy-five percent of the paid earnings ... are exempt if, prior to payment to the employee, they were not subject to an earnings withholding order or an earnings assignment order for support.
derived_from.tier_rationale: Added 2026-08-30 (round 22) to encode the paycheck-tracing exemption the corroboration pipeline's adversarial check found missing -- CCP § 704.070 exempts 75% (or 100%, if already subject to a withholding/support order) of wages actually paid to the debtor within the 30 days before levy and traceable into the account. This is the single most common California bank-levy fact pattern (a recent paycheck sitting in a checking account) and this node previously encoded only the much smaller § 704.220 automatic minimum for it. Confirmed via WebSearch cross-referencing leginfo/Justia/FindLaw mirrors this session; same leginfo web_fetch-timeout caveat as other entries this corpus.

derived_from.quoted_text: Notwithstanding any other provision of this chapter, money in a deposit account of the judgment debtor that is not otherwise exempt under this chapter is exempt to the extent necessary for the support of the judgment debtor and the spouse and dependents of the judgment debtor.
derived_from.tier_rationale: Added 2026-08-30 (round 22) to encode the need-based follow-on exemption the corroboration pipeline's adversarial check found missing -- effective January 1, 2020, this exempts deposit-account money ABOVE the § 704.220 automatic minimum (and not otherwise exempt) to the extent the debtor shows it is necessary for support, ON A FILED CLAIM (not automatic like § 704.220/§ 704.080). No fixed dollar figure -- a fact-specific showing. Same sourcing/caveat as the § 704.070 entry above.

logic.exemption_basis: tied to the Welfare & Institutions Code §11452 'minimum basic standard of adequate care for a family of four, Region 1' figure, as annually adjusted under §11453
logic.note_needs_current_figure: this node encodes the FORMULA and cross-reference verbatim; the actual current dollar figure lives in Welfare & Institutions Code §11452/§11453, which this session did NOT independently pull -- must be looked up current at time of use, not assumed or hardcoded.
logic.automatic: applies without the debtor filing a claim
logic.exceptions: does not apply to a levy to satisfy a judgment for wages owed, child support, or spousal support
logic.determination: money in the debtor's deposit account up to the current W&IC §11452/§11453 figure is automatically protected from an ordinary judgment-creditor levy (not from the carved-out wages/support judgment categories)
logic.public_benefits_note: If the levied account receives DIRECTLY DEPOSITED public benefits or Social Security payments, CCP § 704.080 provides a SEPARATE, larger automatic exemption specific to those funds (roughly $1,750-$2,600 for public benefits, $3,500-$5,250 for Social Security, depending on number of depositors, as most recently adjusted) -- this is in addition to, not instead of, the general § 704.220 minimum this node otherwise encodes. Federal law (31 C.F.R. Part 212) separately requires banks to automatically protect roughly two months' worth of certain federal benefit payments received by direct deposit, independent of any state exemption claim -- flagged as a related federal protection not yet independently encoded here.
logic.aggregation_note: The § 704.220 automatic minimum exemption is a SINGLE aggregate amount across all of the judgment debtor's deposit accounts subject to levy, not a separate exemption per account. A debtor with multiple accounts levied at once (or in sequence) does not get the minimum multiplied by the number of accounts.
logic.natural_person_note: This exemption -- and the CCP § 704 series generally -- is available only to a natural person (CCP § 703.020(a)). An LLC, corporation, partnership, or other entity judgment debtor has no automatic minimum-balance protection under this node.

drafting_revisions.summary: Second pass: added CCP § 704.070 (75-100% recent-wage-deposit exemption), § 704.225 (need-based exemption above the automatic minimum), and a joint-account/third-party-claim note (CCP § 720.110); added 3 corresponding checklist items. First pass (round 21) already added § 704.080/§ 703.020 and the aggregation clarification -- confirmed still present and working in this run's own derivations.

logic.recent_wages_note: If the levied funds are traceable to wages actually PAID to the debtor within the 30 days before levy, CCP § 704.070 separately exempts 75% of those paid earnings (100% if they were already subject to a wage withholding or support-assignment order before payment) -- this is typically far more protection than the § 704.220 automatic minimum alone, and is the most common real-world bank-levy scenario (a recent paycheck). This exemption requires a timely-filed claim, unlike the automatic § 704.220/§ 704.080 minimums.
logic.support_need_note: On a filed claim, CCP § 704.225 exempts deposit-account money ABOVE the automatic minimum to the extent necessary for the support of the debtor and their spouse/dependents -- no fixed dollar cap, fact-specific. This is the routine follow-on claim once the automatic minimum is exhausted; this node should not be read to imply everything above the automatic minimum is unprotected.
logic.joint_account_note: This node treats the levied account as simply 'the debtor's deposit account.' If the account is jointly held with a non-debtor (a spouse, family member, or other co-owner) and some or all of the funds are traceable to the co-owner's deposits, the co-owner may assert a third-party claim of ownership under CCP §§ 720.110 et seq. to recover funds that are not the debtor's -- separately, community-property rules can affect a non-debtor spouse's share differently. This node does not itself perform an ownership/tracing analysis.

completeness_checklist.fact: Current dollar amount of the W&IC §11452 'minimum basic standard of adequate care, Region 1, family of four' figure as most recently adjusted under §11453 -- NOT pulled this session
Whether the underlying judgment being levied is an ordinary debt judgment (exemption applies) vs. a wages/child-support/spousal-support judgment (carve-out, exemption does not apply)
Whether the debtor holds multiple accounts at one or more institutions (CCP § 704.220(e) has aggregation/allocation rules not separately encoded here)

Whether the levied account receives directly-deposited public benefits or Social Security payments (a separate, typically larger exemption under CCP § 704.080 applies in addition to the general minimum, and federal law may independently protect ~2 months of certain federal benefit deposits)
Whether the debtor holds more than one deposit account subject to levy (the automatic minimum is a single aggregate amount across all accounts, not per account)
Whether the judgment debtor is a natural person (this exemption does not protect an LLC, corporation, or other entity debtor's account at all)

Whether the levied funds are traceable to wages actually paid to the debtor within the 30 days before levy (CCP § 704.070 separately exempts 75-100% of those, on a timely claim -- likely the largest protection available for a typical wage earner)
Whether the debtor needs the amount above the automatic minimum for their own or their dependents' support (a fact-specific CCP § 704.225 claim, not automatic)
Whether the levied account is jointly held with a non-debtor whose funds are commingled in it (a co-owner may have an independent third-party ownership claim to part of the balance)

consequences_and_next_steps.action: If a bank account levy does not protect the current W&IC-linked exempt amount for an ordinary debt judgment, object citing CCP § 704.220 -- note the financial institution should apply this exemption automatically without a claim.

(4) A notice that, unless the defendant so responds, their default will be entered upon application by the plaintiff, and the plaintiff may apply to the court for the relief demanded in the complaint, which could result in garnishment of wages, taking of money or property, or other relief.

derived_from.quoted_text: § 415.20 (substituted service): service ... is deemed complete on the 10th day after the mailing. § 415.40 (service outside California by mail): service of a summons by this form of mail is deemed complete on the 10th day after such mailing. § 415.50 (service by publication): the notice shall be published ... at least once a week for four successive weeks; ... service is deemed complete on the 28th day after the first day of publication.
derived_from.tier_rationale: Added 2026-08-30 (round 22) to encode the service-method-dependent completion dates the corroboration pipeline's adversarial check found missing -- this node previously keyed the 30-day answer period to a bare 'date served' without accounting for the fact that substituted, out-of-state-mail, and publication service are all deemed complete LATER than the physical service/mailing date (10 or 28 days later). Applying the deadline from physical service alone understates the true response window by up to 4 weeks for these very common service methods. Confirmed via WebSearch cross-referencing leginfo/FindLaw/process-server-practice sources this session; same leginfo web_fetch-timeout caveat as other entries this corpus.

derived_from.quoted_text: A defendant, on or before the last day of his or her time to plead or within any further time that the court may for good cause allow, may serve and file a notice of motion ... to quash service of summons on the ground of lack of jurisdiction of the court over him or her ... no act by a party who makes a motion under this section, including filing an answer, demurrer, or motion to strike constitutes an appearance, unless the court denies the motion made under this section.
derived_from.tier_rationale: Added 2026-08-30 (round 22) to encode the motion-to-quash alternative the corroboration pipeline's adversarial check found missing -- this node previously framed 'file an answer' as the only response, but a defendant contesting defective service or personal jurisdiction (e.g., sewer service) must instead move to quash under § 418.10; FILING AN ANSWER INSTEAD IS A GENERAL APPEARANCE THAT WAIVES the service/jurisdiction objection entirely. Defective/sewer service is a well-documented problem in consumer debt collection litigation. Same sourcing/caveat as the § 415.20 entry above.

logic.trigger: date the summons is served on the defendant
logic.consequence_of_missing: plaintiff may apply for entry of default and then seek the relief demanded, which can include wage garnishment or other collection remedies
logic.applies_to: the general unlimited/limited civil summons form; California small claims court does not use this summons/answer mechanism (no written answer -- the defendant simply appears on the hearing date) -- that is a separate, not-yet-built node.
logic.service_method_note: The 30-day answer period runs from when service is DEEMED COMPLETE, which depends on the method: personal service is complete on the date of delivery, but substituted service (CCP § 415.20 -- leaving papers with a competent household member/co-worker plus a follow-up mailing) and out-of-state mail service (§ 415.40) are deemed complete 10 days AFTER the mailing, and service by publication (§ 415.50) is deemed complete on the 28th day after first publication. Using the raw date papers were handed over (rather than the deemed-complete date) for substituted/mail/publication service UNDERSTATES the true deadline.
logic.defective_service_alternative_note: 'File an answer' is not the only possible response, and is the WRONG one if the defendant disputes that service or personal jurisdiction were proper (e.g., papers left with someone at an address the defendant doesn't live at, or served on the wrong person). Such a defendant should instead move to quash service under CCP § 418.10 -- a special appearance that preserves the objection. Filing an answer first is a general appearance that WAIVES the service/jurisdiction defense entirely, even if the underlying service really was defective.

completeness_checklist.fact: Date the summons and complaint were actually served on the defendant (not the filing date)
Whether the case is general civil (this node applies) vs. small claims (different procedure, not this node)

The method of service used (personal, substituted, mail, or publication) -- the 30-day period runs from the date service is DEEMED COMPLETE under that method, which can be 10-28 days after the physical service/mailing date for anything other than personal service

Whether the defendant disputes that service was properly made or that the court has personal jurisdiction over them -- if so, the correct response is a motion to quash (CCP § 418.10), not an answer, since answering first waives the objection

consequences_and_next_steps.action: File a written response (Answer or other responsive pleading) with the court within 30 days of the date of service to avoid default.
consequences_and_next_steps.deadline_detail: 30 days from date of service of summons

consequences_and_next_steps.action: If already past 30 days and no default has been entered yet, respond immediately -- courts often still accept a late answer before default is entered.
If a default has already been entered, the available remedy is a motion to set aside the default, not simply filing a late answer -- a separate, not-yet-built node.
